title: One or Two Kinds of Elders?
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Review of Previous Lessons
subpoints: Authority and submission in the church
Models of church government (Episcopacy, Congregationalism, Single Pastor, Presbyterianism)
Christ as the sole head of the church
Equivalence of terms: elder, bishop, and pastor
The necessity of a plurality of elders

outline.title: The Central Question
subpoints: Are there one kind of elder or two kinds?
Differentiation within the office of the elder

outline.title: Historical Views on Eldership
subpoints: Westminster Divines: Three distinct roles (Pastor, Teacher, Ruling Elder)
Ian Murray: Scottish members argued for equal status of ruling and teaching elders
John Calvin: Multiple titles for similar offices (Minister, Presbyter, Bishop, Teacher, Governor)
Charles Hodge: Only ministers are presbyters; ruling elders are a pragmatic, non-scriptural addition

outline.title: Modern Terminology and Application
subpoints: Use of 'staff' and 'non-staff' elders in non-denominational contexts
The need to differentiate between paid and unpaid roles
Tracing historical influences on current church practices

summary:
In this fifth lesson of the Church Government series, Pastor Tito Lyro addresses the theological question of whether the office of elder is singular or divided into distinct categories. The session begins with a review of previous teachings, reaffirming that Christ is the sole head of the church and that a plurality of elders is the biblical standard for local governance, as evidenced in Acts 14:23 and James 5:14. The pastor clarifies that the terms elder, bishop, and pastor refer to the same office, challenging the notion of a single-pastor model.

The core of the sermon examines historical perspectives within the Presbyterian tradition regarding the differentiation of elders. Pastor Lyro contrasts the views of the Westminster Divines, who identified distinct roles for pastors, teachers, and ruling elders, with the arguments of Scottish members like Ian Murray, who advocated for the equal status of all presbyters. He also critiques the 19th-century view of Charles Hodge, who denied the divine origin of ruling elders, labeling them a pragmatic addition rather than a scriptural appointment. This historical analysis highlights the ongoing debate within Reformed theology about the nature and function of eldership.

The lesson concludes by noting how these historical distinctions have influenced modern church terminology, such as the use of 'staff' and 'non-staff' elders in various denominations. By tracing these theological roots, the sermon encourages believers to understand the biblical basis for church governance and the importance of adhering to Christ's appointed structures for the health and order of the local congregation.
